title: The Evening Brief: Ovechkin's Putin ad sparks swift rebuke; sports readies for playoffs
dek: Wednesday's news crystallized a series of divisions: Alex Ovechkin appeared in a pro-Putin campaign ad alongside sanctioned Foreign Minister Lavrov, drawing immediate criticism from Hall of Famer Dominik Hasek and humanitarian José Andrés; meanwhile, across professional sports, rosters locked in final-week positioning as injury attrition mounted heading into October.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The week centered on three colliding currents: a geopolitical statement by the NHL's all-time leading scorer that isolated him from his league's stated values; a cascade of marquee-player injuries that reset expectations for October; and the structural decisions teams made in final days before new labor agreements took effect.
bottom_line: Wednesday and the surrounding days crystallized the sport calendar's preseason inflection point: franchises locked in final structural commitments before labor agreements changed, injuries reset playoff mathematics for at least four NFL franchises, and Ovechkin's campaign appearance raised a geopolitical question the NHL has not yet addressed. The next checkpoints are immediate: whether Garrett, Brown, and Darnold return to action by late September or early October; whether the Dodgers clinch the division by September 18; whether the Yankees rest Judge or increase his playing time in the final regular-season stretch; and whether Ovechkin, the Capitals, or the NHL issue any public statement on the Putin campaign ad.
body: Alex Ovechkin's appearance in a Russian pro-Putin United Russia party campaign advertisement alongside Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, the latter sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury and identified as an architect of Russia's war in Ukraine, marked Wednesday's most immediate tension in professional sports. The commercial, reported by Yahoo NHL based on images in Russian business newspaper Vedomosti, showed Ovechkin standing behind Lavrov alongside other pro-Putin figures including actor Vladimir Mashkov and RT editor-in-chief Margarita Simonyan. Hall of Famer Dominik Hasek and restaurateur José Andrés, who has led humanitarian efforts in Ukraine, condemned the participation. Andrés called it a "sad day for my beloved DC team." Ovechkin has long supported Putin, he founded a pro-Putin social movement in 2017, but when asked about the Russia-Ukraine war, he has said he hopes "it's going to be over" and that he is "not in politics." The NHL has not issued a public statement. Whether the Capitals organization or the league responds will shape how this moment affects the 2026-27 season.

Injury cascades reshaped several franchises' playoff prospects. Myles Garrett, the 2025 NFL Defensive Player of the Year, was placed on injured reserve after knee surgery, meaning he will miss at least four games for the Rams, who mortgaged two future first-round picks and a second to acquire him. A.J. Brown, a three-time Pro Bowl wide receiver, was placed on injured reserve with a high right ankle sprain, sidelining the Patriots for at least four games. Sam Darnold, the Seahawks' starting quarterback, sustained a "very unique" soft-tissue hip injury that the team expects will sideline him short-term but has not specified a timeline. Kyler Murray entered concussion protocol after a hit by Packers safety Javon Bullard. Eagles left guard Landon Dickerson, a three-time Pro Bowl selection, was placed on injured reserve with a bone bruise in his right knee after one game back from surgery. Connor Bedard, named the Blackhawks' captain at 21 on September 15, will not play until November after left shoulder surgery from a July 2 injury. The clustering of these losses in Week 1 compressed the margin for error across multiple contenders during the season's first stretch.

Across professional sports, teams raced against midnight September 16 when a new NHL collective bargaining agreement took effect, capping contract extensions at seven years with current teams, down from eight, and six years in free agency, down from seven. Washington signed Ryan Leonard to an eight-year extension worth $84 million. Colorado locked up defenseman Cale Makar to an eight-year agreement worth $163.2 million at a $20.4 million average annual value, described as the richest in NHL history. The Anaheim Ducks signed Cutter Gauthier to a six-year, $81 million extension with $69.5 million in signing bonuses, front-loaded to exploit the old CBA's structure before it expired. The Minnesota Wild and Montreal Canadiens extended coaches John Hynes and Martin St. Louis to multiyear deals, though both contracts' terms were undisclosed. In the PGA Tour's parallel scramble, the organization outlined its 2028 two-tiered membership structure, locking out LIV players through a 15-PGA-Tour-event-in-2027 requirement that currently excludes all banned golfers. CEO Brian Rolapp reaffirmed there would be no returning-member program like the one offered to Brooks Koepka in January.

On the diamond, the Dodgers clinched their 14th consecutive playoff berth on September 15, tying the Atlanta Braves' all-time record for consecutive postseason appearances. The Brewers clinched their fourth straight NL Central title on September 16, the first franchise in the division's 32-year history to accomplish that feat. The Yankees clinched a third consecutive playoff berth on September 15 when Aaron Judge hit a three-run home run in his first game back from a three-month rib fracture, though he exited Wednesday's 13-inning loss to Minnesota with lower right leg tightness. Pete Alonso hit his 300th career home run on September 16 against his former team, the Mets, becoming the 171st member of that club as Baltimore won 7-5 in extra innings. The Orioles remain in wild-card contention with eight games left.

In women's sports, the WNBA resumed after a three-week FIBA Women's World Cup break with eight teams clinched for the playoffs but seeding unsettled. Minnesota and Golden State are vying for the top seed; a three-team traffic jam between Las Vegas, Atlanta, and Indiana determines home-court advantage at the No. 3 and No. 4 positions. The USA women's basketball team won the FIBA World Cup gold medal against France on September 13, capturing their fifth consecutive title, with Breanna Stewart named tournament MVP.

Structural and governance questions persisted unresolved. Five major men's sports leagues, the NFL, NBA, NHL, MLB, and MLS, sent a joint letter to state gaming regulators on September 15 demanding sportsbooks ban and report bettors who engage in harassment. The WNBA and NWSL were excluded despite documented betting-related harassment of WNBA players, drawing swift criticism from WNBPA executive director Terri Carmichael Jackson. NBA Commissioner Adam Silver cited the Timberwolves' precedent when imposing five first-round draft picks, a $30 million fine, and a one-year ownership ban on the Clippers for salary-cap circumvention involving Kawhi Leonard's compensation; Ballmer accepted without appeal. The Senate voted 74-24 to advance the Protect College Sports Act toward final passage, a bipartisan bill that would cap athlete NIL payments and restore NCAA authority, though labor unions and civil rights groups have opposed it.
